This study introduces a fresh stochastic recurrence relation for the autocorrelation function of the Poisson self-excited process, demonstrating its rapid convergence toward a limiting value. We examine the conditions required for the existence of a stationary solution to a generalized version of this process and derive a novel recurrence relation for its autocorrelation function, whose closed-form solution is obtained. Additionally, we propose methods for estimating both the regression coefficient and the residual excitation parameter in the associated linear combination, specifically targeting the residual self-excited component. These approaches are integrated into a comprehensive time-dependent auto regressive model, for which we detail estimation procedures and a set of diagnostic tools. The proposed framework is applied to model the global daily count of cryptocurrency initial coin offerings. We also developed a simplified linearized variant of the model to generate forecasts and conducted extensive simulations to assess the overall modeling strategy, the specific diagnostic methods, and the forecasting technique. These simulations also helped clarify the conditions under which the time-dependent coefficient can be effectively approximated. The resulting model offers practical insights into initial coin offering activity and serves as a flexible tool for forecasting related events. Keywords: Self-excited process, point process, initial coin offering, stochastic process, time series analysis, forecasting, diagnostic tests, Recurrence Relation. Aerosol scattering between planets and stars contaminates direct imaging efforts aimed at exoplanet detection and characterization. This contamination manifests as photometric dimming in a star's light as it passes through the interstellar medium. Because this dimming occurs outside the region targeted by direct imaging campaigns, it can be utilized to perform local photometric metrology for extreme direct imaging projects. This method has been successfully applied to a series of stars observed by the VICTOR campaign to quantify contamination levels and estimate precision. These precision estimates, in turn, allow for the derivation of absolute scattering efficiencies from the measured dimdings. While the VICTOR technique has been utilized up to this point, it represents a significant leap forward from the legacy of year-long campaigns like PVTX and SHATTEL, achieving this with just a few hours of observational time. Demonstrating that VICTOR can resolve seasonal differential atmospheric refraction errors has also been possible. Additionally, the VICTOR approach has helped identify and characterizing remaining systematic errors from coronagraphic data, as illustrated with the HabEx/SpaceINFRA demo stars. Furthermore, VICTOR has provided constraints on the scattering efficiencies of sizes for previously unmeasured stars. Looking ahead, future projects could potentially use VICTOR-like methods to help characterize the point spread functions of new extreme direct imaging initiatives, such as the HabEx and LUVOIR concepts. Such constraints could be valuable for both scientific operations and for meeting scientific accreditation requirements. Ultimately, the VICTOR method serves as a powerful tool for measuring the radiative properties of interstellar aerosols. This paper outlines the VICTOR technique, highlights its past applications, and discusses potential future uses. Complementary materials offer further details on the method and its applications. This research investigates and enhances the performance of the Langevin Dynamics (LD) algorithm for sampling configurational space in chemical reactions. The study begins with a theoretical examination of LD's dynamics, identifying a previously unrecognized issue: excessive friction degrades sampling efficiency. A novel scaling relation between friction and temperature is proposed to mitigate this problem and boost efficiency. The approach is validated through a case study on the benzene ignition reaction, where the new method demonstrated a tenfold increase in efficiency compared to standard LD. Furthermore, the technique outperformed the underdamped Langevin dynamics (ULSD) method employed by the SHOCK code. These findings indicate that the proposed method offers a robust and efficient alternative to ULSD and other established techniques for modeling chemical reactions. The code is accessible at https://github.com/yangyong99/NoUUnderdampedLangevin. key words: kinetics, Langevin dynamics, friction, efficiency, sampling.

This study investigates the extent to which models trained on human benchmark data, such as VQA and VRD, can leverage existing end-to-end systems optimized for video descriptions, specifically MemAlign and MemoryNetwork. Our findings indicate that for both MemAlign and MemoryNetwork, the training datasets derived from the VB-Bench benchmark exhibit lower accuracy compared to MemBERT and FiBERT when evaluated on the MSVD dataset. Similarly, when applied to the ViseD dataset, MemBERT and FiBERT demonstrated superior performance to the models generated from VB-Bench. These results highlight the significant challenge of creating comprehensive datasets that cover diverse video domains while maintaining high quality. Ultimately, the success of a video description architecture relies not only on its design but also on the volume and variety of available data, as evidenced by the consistent superiority of MemBERT and FiBERT over models trained on smaller benchmarks like MSRVd, MTVs, and ViseD. We achieve a closed-form expression for the central charge intricacy, a non-trivial measure of complexity within conformal field theory, by solving the Sylvester equation $AX+XA^{T}=B$. This accomplishment yields a direct method for calculating the intricacy of any proposed CFT. We observe that the central charge intricacy follows a step-like pattern as a function of $c$. Notably, we identify a range, $-2 < c < 2$, where the intricacy assumes negative values, indicating that the standard definition of intricacy is insufficient for this domain. To resolve this, we extend the notion of intricacy into the complex plane, creating a unified framework applicable across all physically relevant values of $c$. Furthermore, we provide a constructive procedure for determining the intricacy at any specific value of $c$. Regarding the 2D Ising model, $c_{\text{Ising}} = 1/2$, our results confirm its intricacy equals 3, aligning with previous findings. In contrast to earlier approaches, our method does not rely on assuming an affine algebraic nature for $2^{1/2}c$. Finally, addressing the Minkowski scalar-tensor theory with parameter $\xi$, we find its central charge intricacy remains constant for $\xi < 1/6$ but increases step-wise for $\xi > 1/6$, implying that this model is more complex at the previously unexamined region $\xi > 1/6$. The computational code accompanying this work is accessible at https://github.com/aminjafari/EulerArnoldIntricacy. Additionally, this manuscript complements the arXiv paper: arXiv:2302.01601v1 [math-ph] by A. Jafari and F. Gohert-Pesaunen.

This section addresses the prediction of the production cross section for a specific hadron species within a proton-proton ($pp$) collision. The underlying premise relies on the fact that the baryon-to-meson yield ratio ($Y_{B}/Y_{M}$) in $pp$ collisions remains constant and identical to the $Y_{B}/Y_{M}$ ratio observed in proton-antiproton ($p\bar{p}$) collisions at a given center-of-mass energy. This constancy is attributed to the universal nature of hadronization, which dictates that baryon and meson yields depend solely on local physical conditions, specifically the temperature ($T$) and baryon chemical potential ($\mu_{B}$). Utilizing this approach, we calculate the cross section for a particular hadron species in $pp$ collisions. The method involves two steps: first, determining the $Y_{B}/Y_{M}$ ratio through statistical hadronization model fits to baryon and anti-baryon production cross sections; second, applying this ratio to the cross section of the corresponding anti-species to derive the total species cross section. It is important to note that this technique only yields the direct cross section, excluding any contributions from cascade formations. As demonstrated in Section 3, this calculated cross section serves as the input for the simulation framework employed in this work. Our implementation of this method is detailed in Appendix A. The specific cross sections derived for various hadrons using this approach are summarized in Table A.1. Furthermore, we have extended this calculation to hadro-chemical models designed for anti-proton-antiproton ($\bar{p}\bar{p}$) collisions, with the results for individual hadrons listed in Table A.2.

This paper introduces wideband protocols for integrated data and energy delivery (IDED) suitable for single- and multi-antennas with limited capabilities, offering a practical alternative to IDER solutions that demand significant hardware complexity. Through a wideband analysis of the IDER approach, we demonstrate that IDER systems do not consistently achieve higher summed energy delivery (ED) than IDES systems when operating under identical conditions. Furthermore, we establish that the optimal configured number of IDES streams is constrained by both available hardware power headroom and channel conditions. Leveraging a wideband IDES formulation, we develop an efficient iterative algorithm for joint data rate and beamforming matrix optimization. Our numerical results present a comprehensive comparison of the proposed wideband IDES, single-carrier multi-user power-domain multiplexing, and multi-carrier OFDMA gedd policies, highlighting substantial gains for the wideband IDES approach. Finally, we derive an closed-form upper bound for wideband IDES, confirming that it falls short of scaling linearly with bandwidth and remains dependent on the radio frequency power amplifiers' power back-off. An efficient iterative algorithm for minimizing this loss to maximize bandwidth efficiency is also provided. Simultaneously, we observe significant improvements in achievable data rates compared to IDES. These findings underscore the value of pursuing both data rate and ED objectives simultaneously but within distinct user subsets. Additionally, our results indicate that increasing the count of user-groups receiving energy alone yields only marginal ED improvements while causing significant data rate declines for groups simultaneously optimized for data. The derived IDES upper bound and related numerical outcomes further reveal that single-carrier IDES generally outperforms its wideband counterpart in terms data rates, whereas wideband IDES delivers superior energy delivery (subject to total power constraints) and overall IDED system performance. These conclusions support the adoption of single-carrier wideband IDES policies (via beamforming) as a cost-effective solution, particularly when dedicated data and energy-receiving user groups exhibit distinct characteristics.

Fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) represents a complex statistical challenge that demands a comprehensive theoretical and statistical framework. This article outlines the essential components required to perform a rigorous PDF fit, addressing both statistical methodologies and theoretical necessities. While previous fits have effectively utilized Bayesian approaches for ranking and interpolation, this work expands upon these elements and integrates key statistical concepts such as p-values, confidence intervals, and predictive distributions. Additionally, the discussion covers critical theoretical aspects including scheme conversions, order conversions, and PDF expansions. Although this paper concentrates on PDF fitting, the proposed framework is versatile and applicable to other high-precision statistical analyses in high energy physics. To support this approach, a new open-source program named LJETXFitter has been developed to facilitate rigorous PDF determinations. The detailed procedures for executing this framework are documented in a companion article.

This study employs linearized large-eddy simulation to analyze a methane turbulent jet flame reacting to planar acoustic waves. Within this framework, heat release fluctuations are decomposed into homogeneous and inhomogeneous components, with the latter governed by a linearized reaction term. To derive this component, linearized flamelet equations are solved downstream, initialized with local premixed flame conditions and guided by linearized equivalence ratio fluctuations. Consequently, the reaction term activates solely where premixed flames would form, effectively turning on and off in response to local equivalence ratio fluctuations. These linearized reactions are further constrained by physical limits on temperature and species fluctuations. The resulting approach, termed the active flame method, offers a practical solution for turbulent jet fires without requiring pre-existing crossflow velocity or equivalence ratio fluctuations at the inlet. Demonstrating this, the method was applied to a canonical underexpanded jet, revealing that heat release fluctuations peak at the acoustic mode shape corresponding to maximum velocity slip between the jet and ambient air. Furthermore, incohoheneous heat release dominates when the Mach number is low, whereas resonance-driven heat release prevails at higher Mach numbers. Ultimately, this linearized methodology provides a viable tool for investigating acoustic phenomena in turbulent jet fires, potentially guiding the development of active control strategies for wildfire smoke. Keywords: Wildfire, Eddy Flame, Large Eddy Simulation, Acoustics, Fire Smoke, Linearized.

Nonlocal gravity models serve as effective frameworks for investigating the structural stability of neutron stars and potentially other ultra-dense stellar configurations. This work offers a comprehensive review of the constitutive equations used in these models, systematically organizing them and highlighting their connections and potential gaps. We clarify the constitutive relationship employed in hydrodynamic nonlocal gravity formulations and derive the analogous equation for kinetic nonlocal gravity, demonstrating its utility in modeling ultra-dense ions within neutron star cores. Additionally, we detail the constitutive relation adopted in teleparallel nonlocal gravity and derive the corresponding form for metric nonlocal gravity, which has not yet been explicitly established. We apply this relation to a specific nonlocal modification of Einstein-Gauss-Bonnegravity, recently proposed to resolve the initial value singularity in gravitational collapse, to derive the constitutive relation for that model. Furthermore, we derive a constitutive relation for a specific nonlocal $f(R,T)$ model. We emphasize that the mathematical formulation of the inverse operator varies based on the chosen basis—whether general relativity, teleparallel, or nonlocal $R$-models—and on whether one works in real or complex spaces. We provide a table summarizing the constitutive relations across these various models and bases. Finally, we present a simple model of kinetic, metric, nonlocal gravity to illustrate how matter properties, stellar structure, and structural stability depend on the constitutive relation selected for a specific nonlocal modification.

While proton-proton collisions are characterized by low energy density and high entropy, they generate an immense quantity of secondary particles. This phenomenon is illustrated through several rare processes observed at the LHC. These events typically involve forward-produced particles that traverse undetected by central detectors, necessitating specialized experiments designed to analyze this secondary activity. Such processes represent the primary candidate events for searches for new physics beyond the Standard Model, whether through searches for dark matter, heavy resonances decaying into standard model particles, or other mechanisms. Consequently, these events are termed "minority" events, and the related searches are defined as "minority searches." This article examines these processes and their searches, detailing the techniques used to distinguish them from various background sources. It also explores the potential of minority searches in the future, assessing the capabilities of existing detectors for such analyses and determining the requirements for dedicated future experiments.

The detection of a variable X-ray source, possibly a second black hole, near the Galactic Centre has reinvigorated efforts to model the history of accretion onto both stellar-mass black holes and the hypothetical dark objects in Galactic Centre point sources. This paper revisits the analysis of transient X-ray activity in individual systems to explore potential gaps in current understanding. We identify significant biases in previous studies concerning the measured properties of X-ray transients among neutron star systems. These biases specifically affect the apparent frequency of variability gaps between outbursts and the precision of rise time determinations. Addressing these issues reveals that X-ray transients in neutron star systems governed by tidal locking likely occur more frequently than currently estimated. Furthermore, the precision of post-outburst flux measurements near the typical 2--3$\,h$ recurrence limit varies significantly between systems. For $\dot{\X}-1$ and $\dot{\X}-2$, these variations result in different interpreted recurrence intervals, whereas for $\dot{\X}-6$, the interval remains consistent at approximately 1.5 years. At the Galactic Centre, the long quiescence intervals observed in neutron star systems (ranging from 5 to 20 years) present a challenge, unless the mass accretion rate fluctuations responsible for outbursts are more extreme than those seen in other Milky Way X-ray binaries. The presence of a TTV-1 planet orbiting a black hole suggests that X-ray transients in neutron star systems can trigger stellar orbital resonances. Finally, the renewed focus on recurrence intervals highlights the surprising lack of evidence for transients from the two most massive stars at the Galactic Centre, whether defined by inter-outburst gaps or the variability of X-ray flux following specific outbursts. This absence constitutes a significant puzzle, as it contradicts the well-established transient behavior of all other X-ray binaries containing neutron stars or black holes. We conclude by proposing possible resolutions to this issue and outlining future research directions.

Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two separate sets of entities. These structures are frequently depicted as two parallel lines of vertices linked by edges, a format known as a complete layering. Often, the goal is to achieve a complete layering where edge lengths are as uniform as possible, creating a spring-like appearance. This specific type of representation is called a equitable bipartite drawing. Achieving one of these drawings is NP-hard, and we are also looking to minimize the variance in edge lengths. Using the fact that finding an equitable bipartite drawing with a fixed number of edges on one set of parallel lines can be modeled as a minimum weight perfect matching problem on a bipartite graph, we introduce an FPT algorithm to minimize variance while constraining the count of edges between the two sets of vertices on one of the parallel lines. Additionally, we provide an algorithm to generate all equitable bipartite drawings that optimize the variance for any subset of vertices along one set of parallel lines. As extensions, we outline algorithms to induce a drawing that is "nearly" equitable if the optimized one exceeds the maximum feasible edges between the two sets on one set of parallel lines, or if it surpasses the total edges between the two sets of vertices. We apply our FPT method to determine an equitable bipartite drawing for the complete graph $K_n$, where $n$ is a small integer, by decomposing $K_n$ into two complete bipartite graphs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for the complete graph $K_9$, an equitable drawing with 21 edges exists that uses exactly two vertex splits. This result confirms that $K_9$ possesses a nearly equitable drawing with 21 edges. Finally, we offer several open problems related to equitable drawings of bipartite and complete graphs. Our work supports the research of Goddard, Kahl, and Walther on nearly equitable drawings of complete graphs and of Beneyta, Bulteau, Gasparovic, Guo, Hermelin, Joerger, and To for on equitable drawings of complete and bipartite graphs.

Extended degradation of CPU performance serves as a effective strategy to prolong the operational duration of energy-constrained systems. While prior research has primarily focused on prolonging battery life through CPU frequency scaling in mobile devices, there remains a lack of comprehensive studies evaluating the impact of degrading CPU performance from 1 GHz to 2 GHz on both system performance and battery longevity. This research investigates the relationship between system performance and battery extension when CPU frequency is scaled down. The findings indicate that a 50% reduction in CPU frequency results in approximately a 47% decline in overall system performance, yet yields a remarkable 2.6-fold increase in battery life. To evaluate the efficacy of frequency scaling across real-world workloads, we developed HyperDegrade, an automated framework that dynamically selects the optimal frequency level to maximize battery duration for specific tasks. Our results demonstrate that workloads running at 1 GHz via HyperDegrade exhibit significant battery life improvements compared to those operating at higher frequencies. Furthermore, we conducted extensive analyses to identify the key factors influencing battery extension when frequencies are reduced to 1 GHz. Guided by these insights, we implemented an implementation-aware scheduling algorithm that prioritizes battery life extension; testing confirms this approach outperforms existing methods in maximizing battery duration for workloads executed at 1 GHz. Validating the practical utility of frequency scaling to 1 GHz for real-world workloads, our framework automatically designates workloads with the greatest battery life gains to run at this level, while others operate at 800 MHz. Consequently, a mixture of workloads at both 1 GHz and 800 MHz achieves a 19% longer battery life than all workloads running at 900 MHz. To assist system designers in setting maximum frequency limits to maximize battery extension, we conducted additional studies examining the impact of capping the highest allowable frequency. These studies reveal a near-linear correlation between the chosen maximum frequency and the resulting battery life prolongation. Finally, we assessed the feasibility of powering current smartphones solely at 1 GHz, confirming that contemporary mobile devices can operate effectively at this level without experiencing excessive job wait times in the scheduler. To facilitate further research on battery life extension, we released the open-source HyperDegrade framework alongside a detailed dataset containing system performance and battery duration metrics for a wide range of real-world workloads across various CPU frequencies. This dataset is available at https://useuclid.github.io/batdataset/. HyperDegrade is also accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/useuclid/H

This paper introduces a novel local knot operation termed the twist operation, which extends the standard crossing change and resolves the issue of extra twists introduced by the under-over move in the context of invariants derived from trace representations of the braid crossing generator. We demonstrate that the composition of two twist operations at distinct locations is equivalent to the composition of two remote full Twists, a operation known to preserve both classical and welded link invariants. Consequently, we establish that the Twist operation commutes with other elementary local classical and welded link operations, including the classical crossing change (and its inverse), the Y-move, and the detour move. Leveraging the Twist operation, we define a new invariant of classical links that remains constant under the Twist operation and is also invariant under the Y-move; this invariant is constructed from a classical link invariant of welded links that is invariant under the full twist operation. We utilize this new invariant of classical links to show that the Alexander invariant, together with its associated long exact sequence and generators/morphisms, does not serve as an invariant of the fundamental group of classical links under the fundamental group of welded links operation. As an application of our new invariant of classical links, we provide a proof that a specific invariant of classical links derived by Murasugi from the Alexander invariant is also invariant under the operation. Finally, we introduce and investigate additional invariants of classical links based on a invariant of classical links constructed by Frohman, Kauffman, and Levine from the fundamental group of braids under the full twist operation. We conclude by outlining several open problems related to this research. The notations and results presented in this work may find applications in the study of invariants of classical, virtual, and welded links. Potential directions for future research stemming from this work could also benefit the investigation of invariants of knotted graphs, surface knots, and other related topics. Furthermore, some of the results from this work may be relevant to problems in physics concerning the invariants of classical and virtual knots derived from theory. These invariants are employed to address issues regarding the integrability of integrable systems in statistical mechanics, such as the Yang-Baxter equation and the triangle relation, from the perspectives of both classical and virtual knots.

This game theoretic study examines how two teams of agents play a signal detection game on regular graphs, representing either military squads or terrorist cells. Each team aims to minimize its own expected cost function, which depends on the detection rate and energy consumption. The teams possess heterogeneous sensing and communication capabilities and operate with limited information regarding the other team's actions. With no prior knowledge of the regular graph's topology, the teams are unaware of its specific structure. Under the assumption that the graph is regular, each team adopts a synchronization strategy reliant only on the degree of the graph's vertices and their own action's initial direction. We analyze the game when both teams select this assumed regular graph topology Synchronization Equilibrium (RTE) strategy, characterizing the equilibrium strategies and costs for each team's cost function. Finally, we generalize the equilibrium strategies beyond fixed regular graphs to arbitrary graphs and investigate the game's Bayesian Equilibrium. The proposed equilibrium strategies are not necessarily unique, and we derive an algorithm to find a Bayesian Equilibrium for the game on regular graphs.

This paper demonstrates the Cartesian breakdown technique used to embed a direct product of groups as a subgroup within a wreath product. Applying this method, we establish new results regarding the embeddability of direct products of classical and Lie groups, as well as of groups embedded in GL(n,C), into pure and bi-classical wreath products. Consequently, several of the obtained findings extend the work presented in \cite{Agnew2024}. We do not always achieve the most general result possible with this approach; in such cases, we indicate where the Cartesian breakdown step causes limitations and suggest potential directions for future research to address them. The embeddability results derived here via the Cartesian breakdown are complemented by calculations from special linear groups that show these results are optimal up to the specific direct product of groups involved in the "before breakdown" stage. These final calculations also confirm the optimality of the overall results. Additionally, we provide a proof for the optimality of the optimality statement itself. As part of this proof, we establish a novel result: a group direct sum of cyclic components of length at least 7 (or, under certain conditions, 6) can be embedded into $A_5\wr A_3\,(=\,B_2)$ as well as $SL(3,C)\,(=\,X_2)$ as a triangular subgroup, utilizing the standard embedding of $SL(n,C)$ into $SL((n+1)! ,C)\,(=\,X_{n+1})$. Finally, we offer some remarks on an open problem concerning the exact structure of certain "large" optimal direct products of classical groups.

The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by quantum shot noise, a issue shared across all types of interferometric sensors. To address this, we propose a sloshing Sagnac interferometer, an alternative to conventional Michelson interferometers, and demonstrate through both theoretical analysis and experimental use that this design can surpass the limiting high-frequency sensitivity of standard configurations. Our report details the fundamental principles enabling this enhancement, outlines the necessary modifications to the loudspeakers—specifically regarding bandwidth and phase response—required to shift the quantum noise spectrum into a sloshing Sagnac setup, and provides a practical roadmap for implementing this new topology using the advanced actuators currently available at the LIGO detectors. Furthermore, we confirm that a sloshing Sagnac interferometer can be operated with a quantum noise spectrum comparable to a Michelson interferometer equipped with 200 W of circulating power, yet still achieve a 3.6 dB reduction in high-frequency sensitivity. While further optimization of the sloshing Sagnac setup's spectral shape is required to overcome the sensitivity limits of the LIGO Advanced detectors, such improvements are feasible, for instance, by increasing laser power or employing squeezing. Finally, we speculate on the potential of a hybrid system linking a Michelson and a sloshing Sagnac interferometer via a beamsplitter to utilize the sloshing Sagnac's superior high-frequency response, even when powered by lower energies.

Extra-large multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) cellular systems represent a promising solution for addressing the escalating challenge of available spectrum in cell-free random-access (CA) protocols. This study introduces a novel non-intersecting CA (NICA) architecture for XL-MIMO environments, designed to tackle the issue of service region overlap between the small-cell CA and XL-MIMO access regions. By leveraging the directional characteristics of small-cell base stations (SBs), the NICA protocol establishes a small-cell CA zone and an SB invisible region, which is subsequently managed by the XL-MIMO base station. Conversely, the XL-MIMO station also defines its own access region and an SB invisible region, handled by the small-cell SB. The optimal geometry parameters for this non-intersecting setup are determined using genetic algorithms. Simulation results demonstrate that the non-intersecting NICA protocol significantly outperforms existing CA solutions in terms of sum throughput, achieving gains of 2.3x to 3.1x under heavy user loads, while also delivering notable improvements in delay-throughput performance. Furthermore, these results highlight the advantages of the proposed optimal geometry parameters over standard uniform deployment configurations.

Although neural language models have largely replaced $N$-gram models due to superior performance, our findings suggest that $N$-grams still yield higher accuracy in specific scenarios, such as low-resource low-level domains and low-order $N$-grams. This study introduces a hybrid approach where a neural network predicts the residual error of an $N$-gram model to enhance language modeling and generation tasks. Trained without backpropagation, the $N$-gram component reduces memory usage and speeds up inference, while the neural network focuses on learning the remaining errors. Experiments showing this method surpasses standard neural models in low-resource low-level domains confirm the advantages of combining distinct $N$-gram and neural strategies. Our data releases and code are accessible at https://github.com/ChunghyukYim/NeNG.

This study evaluates a system capable of identifying and correcting OCR errors to generate accurate vote counts from ballot images. While commercial OCR solutions offer high overall accuracy, they frequently make specific mistakes, such as confusing visually similar characters (e.g., M and N) or misinterpreting smudged ink as capital letters. These errors can skew tallies and necessitate manual review by election workers. To address this, we introduced iOCR, a character-level neural network trained to detect and rectify errors made by five popular commercial OCR engines. In evaluations using over 30,000 real-world scanned ballots, iOCR was more than twice as accurate as the best-performing commercial engine in predicting the correct character and delivered significant gains across all metrics. Consequently, iOCR can precisely convert text from scanned ballots, ensuring election workers receive accurate data during recounts. The source code and dataset for demonstrating and replicating these results are available at github.com/vicam/ioCR. Additionally, a simplified version of the dataset, restricted to a smaller subset, can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.09214v1 to facilitate the development of further research on this problem.

This study investigates potential planetary atmospheric circulation patterns using a simplified barotropic beta-plane model. While previous research concentrated on geostrophic balances, we also explore cyclostrophic balances, which are anticipated in planets with higher stellar irradiation or faster rotation rates. We confirm the emergence of Gyres, Jets, and Waves, identifying Gyres as the dominant structure when cyoclostrophic effects are significant. Subsequently, these cyoclostrophic balance patterns transition into geostrophic patterns as beta-plane effects become more prominent. Guided by these findings, we develop a simple predictive framework for the dominant circulation patterns based on physical parameters. Specifically, we define a dimensionless parameter $\xi$ (representing the ratio of cyclostrophic to geostrophic effects) and another dimensionless parameter $\Lambda$ (analogous to the Rossby number). This framework predicts that the dominant patterns shift from cyclostrophic to geostrophic as $\xi$ moves from $<1$ to $>1$, regardless of the value of $\Lambda$. Furthermore, the patterns transition from chaotic to ordered (or vice versa) as $\Lambda$ shifts from $<1$ to $>1$, irrespective of $\xi$. These predictions align well with the circulation patterns observed in our model. Finally, these findings offer insights into the atmospheric circulation patterns of exoplanets.

This study presents a novel, self-contained, and fully rigorous derivation of a Kohnell-style multiple integral representation for the reciprocal $\Gamma$ function, grounded in a new regularized recursion relation. Through this approach, we offer a concise and straightforward proof of the fact that no such Kohnell-style multiple integral representation exists for the Gamma function itself. Leveraging the multiple integral formulation, we formulate a conjecture regarding a Riemann-style single integral representation and demonstrate its equivalence to the standard definition. Furthermore, we utilize the multiple integral form to generate a fresh, direct proof of the uniqueness of the conjectured Riemann-style integral representation. In a separate endeavor, we explore an Archimedean multiple integral representation of the reciprocal $\Gamma$s, exploring its potential applications in probabilistic contexts. Ultimately, we establish a connection between this Archimedean representation and the multiple integral representation, thereby yielding a novel, direct, and rigorous proof of the uniqueness of the former when viewed as a distribution. As a final contribution, we define an Eulidian multiple integral representation and illustrate how to derive it from the Archimedean version, finally proving that this Eulidian representation is equivalent to the standard multiple integral expression of the reciprocal Gamma function. Throughout this work, we deliberately refrain from employing complex analysis techniques or any of its associated principles. Hydrodynamic theories provide effective strategies for managing complex systems of interacting particles, such as ultracold atomic gases. These models are especially valuable when solving many-body quantum problems is computationally unfeasible. Although standard hydrodynamics works well near thermal equilibrium, it often fails to describe quantum systems operating far from equilibrium. To address this limitation, we introduce a stochastic method known as phase-space random quantum hydrodynamics (QRHQ). This approach extends hydrodynamic frameworks into the Wigner phase space, enabling the simulation of strongly interacting quantum systems even when they are deep out of equilibrium. We validate this new QRHQ method against rigorous quantum Monte Carlo calculations for a one-dimensional Bose gas and against quantum kinetic theories for both one- and three-dimensional gases. The resulting QRHQ solutions offer detailed insights into non-equilibrium dynamics, highlighting significant variations across different directions in the 1D gas and demonstrating the emergence of thermalization in the 3D gas. Furthermore, when applied to a one-dimensional gas subjected to a sudden change in confinement, the solutions reveal distinct quantum, classical, and stochastic behaviors under varying initial conditions. Ultimately, QRHQ serves as a powerful tool for investigating non-equilibrium dynamics in quantum systems, uncovering details that other theoretical models often miss. Ultimately, this paper presents a stochastic approach to modeling quantum systems within the Wigner phase space, yielding findings with potential relevance for other methods like quantum molecular dynamics. Such cross-methodological discoveries could aid in understanding experiments involving ultracold atoms, for instance, by analyzing sudden confinement changes in one- and three-dimensional quantum gases. Such investigations are conducted at facilities like NASA's Cold Atom Lab on the International Space Station, where microgravity conditions allow for the creation of larger, colder atomic clouds.

An artificial intelligence system capable of acquiring human knowledge serves as the foundation for many educational applications. Traditional knowledge learning methods, primarily based on neural networks, have relied on deep student networks (S-networks) to process vast volumes of data. However, training deep S-networks by connecting them to data presents significant challenges. To address this, the paper-based architecture introduces an instructor-student framework, where the S-network is supplemented by an instructor network that guides learning. This work examines recent advancements in this architecture, detailing how networks are constructed, the knowledge acquisition workflow, and potential applications. Distinct from prior surveys focused on conventional deep learning, this survey specifically targets the in-school instructor-student architecture. We propose a unified framework to clarify architectural variations, consolidate learning protocols, and categorize tasks into three categories: knowledge construction, adaptation, and aggregation. Based within this framework, we classify tasks and corresponding approaches. Furthermore, we analyze the strengths and limitations of the instructor-student architecture for specific tasks like knowledge construction and aggregation. To guide future research, we identify open issues and potential directions for evolving this architecture. Ultimately, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of in-school knowledge learning via the instructor-student architecture, offering valuable insights and a clear roadmap for future investigative efforts. Taking the square of the field as the basis, we introduce a compact algebraic representation for undirected graphical models. We demonstrate that this representation significantly enhances the computational efficiency of inference algorithms, specifically highlighting its benefits for finding optimal solutions in optimisation tasks. Using a combination of theoretical proofs and empirical experiments, we establish that this new approach accelerates exact most probable edge cutting (MPEC) and most probable trail (MPT) algorithms, thereby advancing restricted maximum likelihood estimation in graphical models. Furthermore, we apply this representation to introduce a simpler, more direct algorithm for constrained optimisation, improving upon current methods by up to an order of magnitude. Collectively, these findings provide a practical framework for exploring potentially expensive strategies to make graphical models more sparse and directly connecting such structures to both exact most probable cutting/trail algorithms and constrained optimisation approaches. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/Chetlakha/FAST. Keywords: probabilistic graphical models, most probable edge cutting, most probable trail, constrained optimisation, compact representation, exact methods.

The recently introduced higher rank Racah algebra $R(n)$ is reviewed, followed by the definition of a quotient algebra by central elements termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$. Leveraging classical invariant theory, it is demonstrated that $sR(n)$ is isomorphic to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ corresponding to the diagonal embedding of $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)^{\otimes n}$. This isomorphism yields a novel presentation of $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ via generators and relations. Furthermore, it is established that the Hilbert-Poincaré polynomial of $sR(n)$ (and consequently $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$) satisfies a recurrence relation governed by the second Bessel polynomial. This recurrence is utilized to compute the coefficients of the Hilbert-Poincaré polynomial for $Z_{3}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, revealing that the special Racah algebra $sR(3)$ is isomorphic to the Lie super algebra $gl(3|1)$. Additionally, the coefficients indicate that $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ possesses infinite dimension for all $n\geq4$. Finally, the isomorphism between $sR(n)$ and $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is employed to derive a new algebraic identity involving the 3-Racah matrix.

Statistically significant A/B testing is essential for determining if the performance differences between two algorithms are genuine. While data scientists frequently employ p-value-based methods to compare the scores of A and B algorithms between groups, they often rely on permutation testing implemented via random sampling. Although sampling works for small datasets, it becomes computationally infeasible for large ones. To address this challenge for structured test statistics where valid tests are difficult to obtain, we introduce PRECISSE, a precise paired-permutation testing framework. We demonstrate PRECISSE's efficacy and feasibility through various real-world scenarios and contrast it with sampling-based approaches. Additionally, we provide a practical guide for implementing PRECISSE with real-world data. The necessary code is accessible at https://github.com/hao-chen-ucb/PRECISSE.

Using the AMPT multiphase transport model, we re-examine the connection between the triangular flow $v_3$ and initial state fluctuations in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Our results indicate that below $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV, initial state higher-order anisotropies, particularly $e_3$, exhibit greater sensitivity to center-of-mass energy variations than $v_3$. Conversely, at 200 GeV, the dependence of $v_3$ on initial state anisotropy $e_3$ varies significantly across different multiplicity measures, a phenomenon directly influenced by the centrality definition employed. Furthermore, $v_3$ demonstrates a clearer prominence at partonic anisotropies. These findings underscore the necessity of employing multiple initial state anisotropy metrics and multiplicity metrics when analyzing the elliptic flow $v_2$ and $v_3$. Ultimately, our study highlights that the EHD mechanism exerts a more substantial impact on $v_3$ than on $v_2$.

Soccer is an ideal domain for applying deep reinforcement learning (DRL) technologies, which have shown significant success in this sport. This study introduces a hierarchical dual agent critic (HDAC) algorithm specifically designed for critical moments of matches. By integrating game theory with soccer-specific knowledge, the model first evaluates match states to determine whether a team should attempt a riskier action like a counterattack or play for a goal in the final minutes, considering the current score and remaining time. Consequently, the HDAC agent selects the most appropriate team action based on this context. The research describes this work in detail, illustrating how the algorithm utilizes remaining match time and score differences to derive the optimal action. The methodology begins by converting time-related data into discrete steps and employing game theory to assess the expected remaining points (ERP) for both teams. Furthermore, the approach introduces a hierarchical structure where two DRL agents are employed: one to choose the correct ERP target (either higher or lower) and a second to select the specific action required to achieve that target. As a final enhancement, the system incorporates a mechanism to boost the probabilities of actions occurring in the last few minutes of the game. Experimental results from open datasets demonstrate that the proposed HDAC method outperforms existing approaches, achieving higher mean squared errors and mean costs compared to baseline models. These findings confirm the algorithm's effectiveness in selecting optimal actions during decisive moments, ultimately contributing to the broader goals of soccer analytics and the development of soccer robots. This study reports on the extension of the single-point Laser Doppler Vibrometer (LDV) technique to generate 2D measurements for rotating blades using telecommunication fibers. The proposed method comprises two phases: initially, a spinnable 2D map is created; subsequently, the actual 1DSP (single-point) LDV is replaced by a fiber optic cable for live monitoring. Validated with a turbine featuring seven blades, the system successfully tracked all rotating blades, delivering two datasets per revolution: one from the LDV and another from the optical fiber. This dual-datastream approach enables real-time verification of the target's rotational speed and confirms the completion of the full 2D measurement cycle. Demonstrating that a high-speed, single-location sensor can be substituted with a slower, distant one, this finding holds significant value for industries dealing with high-speed rotating components. Furthermore, the concept could be adapted to employ multiple fiber-optic lines to monitor several components simultaneously.

This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of the spectral and orbital stability for the standing wave solutions of the $\Psi$-Schr\"odinger and Klein--Gordon equations, which result from multiplying the equation with an anharmonic oscillator potential. An explicit formula for the spectrum of the linearized operator acting on the relevant functional space is derived. The findings are applied to assess the spectral and orbital stability of solutions to the $\Psi$-Schr\"odinger and Klein--Gordon equations coupled with an anharmonic oscillator potential. Notably, when the mass parameter of the anharmonic potential is sufficiently large, the spectral and orbital stability of the ground state for the Schr\"odinger equation contradicts the expectation that "virial identities should hold." Consequently, a contradictory pair of virial identities is established for the scenario where the $\Psi$-Schr\"odinger and Klein--Gordon equations are coupled with an anharmonic oscillator potential, particularly when the mass parameter is large enough and the initial conditions correspond to the ground state. These results contradict one another, revealing that virial identities are not invariant under gauge transformations in the presence of an anharmonic potential. This phenomenon mirrors the contradiction between the contradictions reported in Refs. \cite{CRT} and \cite{W} regarding the validity of virial identities and their counterparts in the context of an anharmonic potential, demonstrating that such identities depend on the regularized numerical computation scheme when an anharmonic potential is involved. The conclusions align with those in Ref. \cite{CRT}, confirming that both the virial identities and the contradiction arising between them and the source of the contradiction in Ref. \cite{W} are contingent upon the specific regularization method used for an anharmonic potential. These discoveries highlight the significance of avoiding the use of virial identities when investigating the long-term dynamical behavior of $\Psi$-Schr\"odinger and Klein--Gordon equations with an anharmonic potential. Instead, this work proposes an alternative approach to demonstrating blow-up, as detailed in this study, which relies directly on the initial condition conditions rather than dependent on the derivation of virial identities.

At colliders, neutral particles that traverse the detector may either remain undetected or produce dislocation patterns when interacting with the beam pipe. These particles, whether they are neutrinos or light dark sector candidates like axion-like particles (ALPs), can be studied by analyzing meson decays that yield two collimated neutral systems. This approach, which we term "double-forward" decay searches, has recently been employed by NA62 to investigate charged current neutral meson decays to enable the derivation of stringent limits on rare $K$ decay modes. Building on this concept, we detail how such searches can be applied at Belle II to establish limits on the branching fractions of specific $B$ meson decay modes. Additionally, assuming the existence of an light dark sector, we outline potential discovery-level searches at Belle II for ALPs and other dark sector candidates arising from $B$ meson decays. Ultimately, we emphasize that combining searches based on actual detection with those relying on dislocation patterns—either at the same experiment or across different collider experiments—can significantly enhance sensitivity in identifying these particles. Such synergistic searches have recently been explored by FASER$\nu$/TAØØT at Fermilab and M³L$\beta$ at Belle II for neutrinal interactions in the beam pipe, as well as by AFOSS at Fermilab and Tri@FASER$\nu$ at CERN for pion decays before their neutrinos encounter the beam pipe. Looking ahead, we suggest that similar searches involving particle decays before their products enter a calorimeter or magnet could be implemented at the SuperKEKB upgrade (Belle II), the High-Luminosity LHC (ATLAS and CMS), and the Forward Physics Experiment at FASERx2.

This study evaluates contextualized embeddings from state-of-the-art transformers to detect semantic alteration (SA) in titles and abstracts of scientific articles. Although contextualized embeddings have been widely adopted for SA tasks, there remains uncertainty regarding whether specific model architectures offer measurable advantages over others for this purpose. Furthermore, it remains unclear if embedding dimensions, title-length normalizations, or other factors yield significant gains for tasks like title change detection. To address these issues, we conducted extensive experiments on a new dataset, Contextualized Language Models for Semantic Alteration Detection: Our Dataset And Lessons Learned (CLASAD), using 14,800 papers from Computer Science, Mathematics, and Linguistics. The findings of these experiments are detailed in this work.

A key conclusion from our study is that for many NLP tasks, selecting the most appropriate model is less critical than implementing sound data preprocessing, ensuring high data quality, and adopting sound statistical modeling techniques. These lessons are relevant not only for detection tasks but also for generative tasks, where evaluating contextualized embeddings for semantic changes before and after text generation is essential. Ultimately, our data and insights will assist researchers in leveraging these embeddings to compare the semantic alteration detection capabilities of various models across numerous studies, potentially reducing the use of regressive models like BERT for SA detection in favor of dense vector-based models such as MultiEcec. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/DeepXLab/Contextualized_Embeddings_SAD.

The masses and spins of black holes powering Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) and producing jets are primarily determined through relativistic spin measurement and relativistic radio/X-ray variability. While a relativistic radio lobes model has recently been supported by the correlation between black hole mass and the scale of perpendicular radio lobes, an alternative anisotropic inverse Compton scattering model has also been proposed to explain these lobes. Regardless of the specific model adopted, the mass and spin parameters of AGN black holes will be precisely determined in the coming years. Once established, these parameters will be critically applied to investigate the formation mechanisms of supermassive black holes and their subsequent evolutionary pathways. Furthermore, the spin and mass of these black holes can serve as fundamental parameters for exploring physical phenomena within the vicinity of the event horizon and analyzing the properties of ultra-light scalar particles. If the spin values of AGN black holes fall within a specific range, they indicate the existence of an ultra-light boson, though this would imply the presence of multiple boson species given the known spins of black holes with different masses. By combining the spin and mass of an individual AGN, one can derive a single upper limit for the ultra-light boson's mass; utilizing the "best-fit" spin (which is typically less than one) yields a corresponding lower limit for the boson mass, thereby defining a precise mass range. Furthermore, by employing the derived upper and lower mass limits for an individual AGN, it is possible to calculate the minimum and maximum distances from the event horizon where the ultra-light boson would form. Consequently, this approach allows for the estimation of the minimum boson mass required for the black hole to collapse into a boson star. Ultimately, the mass and spin parameters of supermassive black holes driving AGNs and exhibiting radio lobes will be accurately determined in the future, providing crucial insights into the nature of ultra-light particles. This paper outlines these principles and summarizes relevant recent studies. We begin by determining the mass and spin of the supermassive black hole in M87, proceeding to calculate the mass range of an ultra-light boson based on M87's parameters, and finally, we propose methods for identifying the minimum and maximum masses of such bosons utilizing the mass and spin of any specific AGN.

We implemented a novel approach for simulating driven quantum harmonic oscillators via real-time path integrals on a discrete lattice, employing both Metropolis and heat-bath Monte Carlo algorithms. Following this implementation, we conducted extensive simulations to evaluate the algorithms' performance across various conditions. The results indicate that the Metropolis method converges more rapidly under specific scenarios, whereas the heat-bath algorithm demonstrates superior convergence in others. These findings provide practical guidelines for selecting the most effective algorithm based on the desired initial state and target steady-state characteristics. Ultimately, this work serves as a foundation for applying these techniques to more complex systems that require optimization of the lattice discretization and real-time stochastic sampling to generate quantum fluctuations. Hooplex extends the language of expectations from first-order logic to a quantitative framework for reasoning about programs, grounded in linear ordered semirings. This generalization enables the use of aggregating expectations, a capability essential for various program analyses such as interprocedural constraints, probabilistic expectations, and game-theoretic expectations. Building on leeps (linear expectations), RelHOI(les) introduces an extension of classical first-order intuitionistic reasoning with expectations, incorporating identity, function, and modality operators. Furthermore, RelHOI(les) adds constructive and constructive-negation relational predicates necessary for invariant induction and relational reasoning. In this work, we develop a proof theory for a quantum variant of RelHOI(+), named QRHOI(+), which utilizes a constructive-negation-based relational semantics for invariants. We based this proof theory on a calculus of quantum expectations with affine, boolean, and relational operators, employing a semantics derived from a monoidal closed quantum order semiring. The proof theories for both the les and I(+) variants rely on a semantics of first-order intuitionistic logic with expectations drawn from a monoidal closed quantum ordered semiring. Our proof theory for QRHOI(+), however, is relational and constructive-negation based, utilizing a semantics from an affine monoidal closed quantum semiring equipped with an involution and an additive operator. Within this relational proof theory, we distinguish between "smaller" and "larger" hypotheses to formulate a refinement-style correctness criterion for hoc proofs. We also present a proof theory for a quantum calculus of separation logic with expectations, QSLE(+), and demonstrate the interconnectivity of QRHOI(+), RelHOI(+), and QSLE(+). Regarding applications, we extend invariant induction to handle while loops in QRHOI(+), and we define a proof theory for a quantum variant of refined Hoare logic with expectations, QRhOI(+), which combines relational, refinement, and Hoare logic principles. We conclude by outlining future research directions. Key terms: Hoare logic, relational reasoning, invariant induction, while loops, expectation, quantum logic, separation logic, refinement, quantum programs.

This study addresses the bias—manifesting as physical impossibilities—in the vector magnetic field measurements derived by the NLC vector mode algorithm from solar VSHV data. While the root cause of this bias remains unclear, its presence undermines the reliability of the inversion algorithm for scientific analysis and invalidates the use of this inversion for operational solar vector magnetic field forecasting. Although the specific source of this bias in the solar VSHV data inversion remains unidentified, a similar issue was previously observed in a different solar magnetic field inversion by the speaker (Brookes), located at a distinct solar location and within a separate algorithm. Given that this problem persists across multiple solar inversion algorithms, at various solar regions, and under differing magnetic field conditions, it suggests a more fundamental cause. We propose that the underlying issue stems from how vector mode spectroscopic signals are utilized to determine the solar magnetic field direction. Furthermore, we outline a potential solution to this problem and highlight several challenges that must be overcome to implement it. Keywords: Sun: magnetic fields; Sun: vector magnetic field inversion; Sun: spectropolarimetry; techniques: spectral analysis.  (Abstract)

For any finite classical group $G$ acting on a space of dimension at least 3, the cartier subposet composed of reducible involutions and the group itself is not a lattice; however, its closure within the full subposet of the identity and all involutions does form a lattice. This paper offers combinatorial descriptions of the sets of primes and associated functions for the lattice of involions denoted by $I(G)\le G$, as well as for the complement of the boolean lattice of subspaces within $I(O(n))$. These characteristics are utilized to establish combinatorial formulas for a characteristic function defined on the lattice of all involutions. Furthermore, we provide explicit combinatorial expressions for the Möbius function $\mu(I,I)$ and the absolute value of the Möbius function $|\mu(I,I)|$, where $I$ represents an involution. The characteristic function and the Möbius function serve as fundamental tools for deriving equivariant topological invariants, most notably the Euler characteristic. As an application of the combinatorial formula for $\mu$, we determine the Euler characteristic of the set of regular involutions within the orthogonal group $O(2n)$. Additionally, we present a table detailing the Euler characteristics of the involutions for classical groups ranging from $O(8)$ to $Sp(8)$. Ultimately, we demonstrate that for a finite classical group $G$ and dimension $d$ satisfying $d\ge 3$, the Euler characteristic of the poset of involutions $I(G)$ equals zero.

In the context of semi-Riemannian geometry, a classic result by Darboux and Serret establishes that for curves in Euclidean space, the conditions of being Bertrand or proper-geodesic are equivalent to being circular or a geodesic line, respectively. This study explores these same properties regarding timelike Bertrand curves within Minkowski space. Specifically, we demonstrate that a timelike curve in Minkowski space $\mathbb{R}_1^{n+1}$ ($n \geq 2$) is a timelike helix if and only if it is a timelike Bertrand curve with constant curvature and torsion, satisfying the constraint $g(\N,\W)=0$. Furthermore, we prove that a timelike curve in $\mathbb{R}_1^{n+1}$ is a timelike-GBERD curve if and only if it is a timelike-HEBERD curve with constant curvature and torsion, and we provide a characterization of timelike-GBERD curves in Minkowski space. Additionally, we examine how timelike-BERD curves in this environment relate to their congruent counterparts. The main contribution of this work is the generalization of Fermanian's result from Euclidean to semi-Riemannian space: a timelike-HEBERD curve in $\mathbb{R}_1^{n+1}$ is a timelike-GBERD curve precisely when its curvatures $\k_1$ and $\k_2$ satisfy the condition $\frac{\k_1^2-\k_2^2}{\k_1\k_2}=c$, where $c$ is a non-zero constant and the curvatures are also non-zero constants. We also generalize other related findings. Throughout this paper, we utilize the Frenseri-Serret formula for timelike curves in semi-Riemannian space. Although deep classification networks have been extensively studied, selecting the optimal loss function remains a challenging open problem. This study conducts a comprehensive evaluation of different loss functions for convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and attention-based models, specifically comparing categorical cross-entropy (CCE) with its variants: Focal Loss (FL), Generalized Cross Entropy (GCE), and Entropic Loss (EL). The evaluation framework involves a multi-class dataset with highly unbalanced classes, represented by both raw counts and weights (W), alongside a standard Imagenet set. Findings indicate that for the multi-class dataset, GCE and FL consistently outperform CCE, with GCE+Weight further surpassing other combinations. On the Imagenet dataset, GCE and FL generally yield superior results compared to CCE. Furthermore, when applied to the multi-class data, GCE and EL demonstrate greater robustness to hyperparameter variations than CCE, GCE, and FL. Ultimately, this research confirms that GCE and FL are effective alternatives to traditional CCE, particularly in datasets characterized by class distribution imbalances.

This resource facilitates the training and evaluation of different if-then reasoning models across various datasets and enables the synthesis of multi-modally grounded textual outputs. Furthermore, ATOMIC supports the training of models capable of generating factually and syntactically correct open-ended descriptions for images and videos, potentially serving as a foundational step for downstream tasks involving image/video understanding and textual reasoning. Furthermore, ATOMIC allows for the training of models that generate hypertext links and images or videos based on statements, potentially aiding the creation of personally customized or professionally oriented wikis and blogs. By providing access to syntactically explicit if-then representations, ATOMIC also aids in evaluating the potential for syntactically correct natural language generation. Demonstrating its utility, we trained models using the ATOMIC dataset to generate syntactically correct descriptions for images, videos, and wiki statements. Evaluations confirm that these models can also produce syntactically accurate hypertext and if-then statements. Additionally, we trained models on the ATOMIC dataset to answer if-then questions in the form of yes/no responses or textual explanations; these models were evaluated on two datasets of if-then questions with standard formatted answers, showing potential for converting yes/no questions into if-then format and vice versa. This paper introduces a framework for deep learning-based video prediction from newly acquired views, addressing the challenge of generating frames from angles that were not present in the training data. We hypothesize that a network capable of predicting videos from new views must operate with a dual-representation to manage both seen and unseen views. Consequently, we propose a model with two distinct components: one handling new views through an encodable format and the other managing old views via a directly accessible representation. Consequently, the first component predicts the second. We developed a model employing encoder-based prediction for new views and direct prediction for old views, successfully generating predictions for unseen angles. To evaluate this approach on data from unknown sources, we introduced a novel metric called the new-view metric. The results demonstrate that this methodology effectively predicts videos from new views, achieving state-of-the-art outcomes on standard datasets. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/AbdulrahmanKhan1999/Dual-View-Video-Prediction. In conclusion, this work provides a practical solution for predicting videos from new views, with potential applications in automotive industries, robotics, and related sectors.

The metric dimension of a graph $G$, denoted by $\beta(G)$, represents the size of its smallest resolving set. Recently, we introduced the concept of the trimmed metric dimension for a graph $G$, defined as the metric dimension of $G$ after removing specific isolated vertices from its resolutive graph $\mathcal{R}(G)$. In this paper, we establish upper bounds for the trimmed metric dimension of paths, cycles, and various combinations of these graphs. Furthermore, we determine the exact value of the trimmed metric dimension for paths and all cycles. We also introduce several families of graphs that demonstrate the tightness of the derived upper bounds. Additionally, we define a new invariant, the resolving index of $G$, analogous to the index of a graph $G$, which is twice the number of edges in $G$. We derive upper bounds for this index based on the order and trimmed metric dimension of $G$, and we characterize the graphs that attain these bounds. Finally, we present a lower bound for the trimmed metric dimension of $G$ as a function of its resolving index. The results presented herein extend the application of the metric dimension to specific graph invariants and serve as a useful tool for future research in this area. Regarding notation, for a graph $G=(V,E)$, we let $n(G)=|V|$ and $m(G)=|E|$ represent the number of vertices and edges, respectively. Additionally, $P_n$ and $C_n$ denote the path and cycle graphs with $n$ vertices, respectively. For a subset $S\subseteq V$, we define $G[S]=(V,E(S))$ as the subgraph of $G$ induced by $S$, where $E(S)=\{uv\in E:u,v\in S\}$. Finally, for a vertex $v$ in $G$, $N[v]$ and $N(v)$ represent the closed and open neighborhoods of $v$ in $G$, respectively. This work was created by an AI chatbot.

This study presents a new end-to-end deep learning framework for heart sound categorization that addresses both additive and convolutional noise. The proposed model integrates a hybrid attention mechanism with dual attention blocks into an enhanced Convolutional Neural Network (CC-DA-Net). Specifically, the framework employs Dual Channel and Dual Scale global attention mechanisms within its dual attention blocks. Mathematical models of epidemic dynamics serve as a crucial bridge between theoretical insights and practical actions during both current crises and preparedness phases. In the midst of the present global outbreak caused by the novel coronavirus (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome-2; SARS-CoV-2), models have been extensively utilized to generate predictions for policymakers and regulators regarding the epidemic's trajectory and the potential impacts of various intervention strategies. This article provides a comprehensive review of epidemic models applicable to the current SARS-CoV-2 crisis, examining their foundational assumptions, inherent limitations, and specific uses. We also address common misconceptions surrounding these models and their outputs. While there is no ideal model capable of fulfilling every possible goal for any given epidemic, the selection of a model should be guided by the specific objectives at hand, the available data, and the necessary computational requirements. Although the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic will eventually subside, the lessons learned from its utilization will be invaluable for future infectious disease challenges. Ultimately, during any epidemic, models will remain a central component of the response, whether the ultimate decision involves taking no action or implementing the most stringent interventions available.

It remains uncertain if stellar mass concentrations, specifically supermassive black holes (SBH) and nuclear star clusters (NSC), contribute differently to the flattening of the star-formonemass ($M_*$ - SFR) relation at high masses. Using the JADE2 catalog derived from IR data for 20 million galaxies with $log(M_*/M_{\odot})$ ranging from 8.25 to 11.75, we examined the influence of starlight originating outside the central 100pc on the turning over of this relation at high masses. Our results indicate that the turning over is primarily driven by the non-linear increase of stellar mass at high masses—particularly when light outside the central 100pc is considered—rather than by a corresponding linear decline in specific star formation rate (sSFR). Consequently, both the $M_*$ - sSFR and $M_{BH}*-sSFR$ relations exhibit a much weaker trend, characterized by a broad plateau-like behavior at high masses when the contribution from the central 100pc is accounted for. To precisely determine the point where the $M_* $ - sSFR relation turns over at high masses, future studies should utilize detailed structural analyses and confirm these findings with future high-resolution data from the JWST. Ultimately, once the exact turnover mass is established, broader samples can be employed to investigate the physical mechanisms linking the turnover in the $M_* $ - sSFR relation to the transition between inside-out and outsize star formation patterns, as well as to the turnover in the $M_* $ - NUV color relation at high masses. This study reports on the X-ray properties of the ultra-fast rotating black hole candidates XTE 1590-280 and 4U 0900-10. Both systems exhibit a Type-A hard-to-soft state transition at a luminosity of $3.0 \pm 0.2 E2$ erg/s, which aligns with the Blandford-Payne mechanism. For XTE 1590-280, the inner unstable orbit corresponds to an angular velocity of $0.55 \pm 0.01$ times the Keplerian frequency, indicating that the accretion disk extends to the innermost stable circular orbit, with no evidence for a sub-Keplerian outer disk. Conversely, 4U 0900-10 displays a significant outer sub-Keplerian component, suggesting the disk does not reach the innermost stable circular orbit. These findings challenge standard binary black hole spin evolution models, implying that the angular momentum of 4U 0900-10's donor star is underutilized and that XTE 1590-280 possesses excess angular momentum. Consequently, the formation history of these systems remains unclear, pointing towards atypical channels such as stellar tidal disruption, stellar collapse, or the accretion and/or merger of a companion. Notably, both systems show evidence of at least one consumed low-mass companion, which could explain the anomalous angular momentum issues; however, the innermost orbit frequencies provide constraints on the timing of these consumption events. Alternatively, if these systems were formed via standard hierarchical channels without consuming companions, new mechanisms for angular momentum transport across the disk or onto the donor star would be required. Ultimately, the spin evolution of these ultra-fast rotating black holes offers valuable insights into the fundamental physics of the event horizon, the circumdisk, and the donor star. The key data supporting this work will be analyzed by the TETRO collaboration using NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Telescope, with additional observations conducted by various other facilities.

Synthetic data serves as a crucial resource for developing algorithms on hard-to-acquire datasets, such as medical imaging. While Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have achieved success in specific domains, applying them to medical data remains challenging due to the complex nature of that imagery. Furthermore, existing GAN-based methods are computationally intensive and struggle to generate high volumes of data from complex datasets. In this study, we introduce a Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (PVAAE) framework tailored for brain injury datasets. By initially focusing on low-frequency information to capture global data characteristics before gradually incorporating high-frequency details to refine local features, PVAAE effectively handles brain CT images. This approach not only enhances the fidelity of generated samples but also prepares the model for even more complex brain injury datasets. Evaluations on two brain CT datasets demonstrate that PVAAE outperforms both VAE and GAN architectures in key metrics: it achieves higher fidelity as measured by Fréchet Inception Score (FIS) and Inception Score (IS), improves data utility for classification tasks, and efficiently processes large-scale brain injury datasets. These results confirm PVAAE's superior performance regarding data fidelity, utility, and processing efficiency. The source code is available at: https://github.com/yuhengbo/PVAAE.

Feature extraction serves as an effective strategy for addressing data scarcity in deep learning applications. Given the surge in unlabeled data, the field of Contrastive Learning has gained significant traction for leveraging such data to solve classification tasks. However, existing methods are predominantly problem-specific, resulting in a fragmented landscape that hinders practical deployment and comparative analysis. This paper introduces a unified framework grounded in the contrastive learning principle for classification problems involving unlabeled data. At its core, the approach begins by generating augmented versions of unlabeled datasets through specific transformation functions. It then applies positive and negative contrastive losses: the former aligns original and transformed data points, while the latter separates semantically unrelated pairs. Notably, our framework requires no specific order for these losses and can integrate multiple transformation functions and classes simultaneously. We evaluated this system across 14 datasets spanning text, image, and tabular domains. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms various existing contrastive learning approaches on most datasets. Furthermore, the framework is flexible enough to incorporate any transformation function, such as BERT embeddings, to solve classification problems based on learned representations. Code for implementation is available at: https://github.com/Dr-Ahad-Hashmi/UniContrastive.

Although large language models (LLMs) achieve human-comparable performance in many tasks, integrating structured knowledge remains a cost-effective method for enhancing specific domains. Furthermore, SIVF can integrate multiple knowledge sources simultaneously. Evaluations show that Llvf-7B, our distilled version of Llama-2-7B, achieves state-of-the-results in multiple benchmarks using minimal computational resources.
