We derive the Unruh-Wald volume law for the causal horizon of a global causal horizon (GCH) utilizing the Unruh effect and Wald's volume approach. Our findings indicate that the global temperature arises from the global causal horizon rather than the event horizon, a conclusion supported by a detailed analysis of global heat flow. Furthermore, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between the global temperature and entropy, demonstrating that the first law of thermodynamics holds for the global causal horizon as well. These results suggest that the global temperature and entropy are determined by the global causal horizon, UNR≠HU, and the UNR-Wald volume law, offering fresh insights into the Unruh effect and the thermodynamics of non-linear charged Anti-de Sitter black holes. Additionally, we investigate the phase transition of the non-linear charged Anti-de Sitter black hole, revealing that its global temperature exhibits two distinct phases. Finally, we confirm that the global entropy-monotone increase principle is satisfied across both temperature phases. These results provide new perspectives on the Unruh effect and thermodynamics, suggesting that the global temperature and entropy of non-linear charged Anti-de Sitter black holes differ from those associated with the event horizon. Consequently, the event horizon is not the true horizon of black holes; instead, the global causal horizon serves as the actual horizon, while the event horizon functions merely as a boundary of darkness. This work also deepens our understanding of the UNR-Wald volume law and the "no drama" principle at the global causal horizon.

We present an experimental study aimed at detecting entanglement modifications during control parameter changes within the electron tomographic framework. This approach offers complementary insights to standard measurements, potentially revealing entanglement alterations that are otherwise difficult to observe. Additionally, we demonstrated the capability to identify the transition from classical to quantum behavior in tomographic representations. We also highlighted the visibility of quantum synchronization in single-electron systems via their tomograms. These concepts were applied to the W state, a non-additive entangled state characterized by partially degraded entanglement across its modes. In the corresponding tomograms, this degradation manifests as increased noise. Our findings indicate that entangled features persist in the tomograms even when entanglement has vanished in the underlying quantum states, suggesting that tomograms can highlight entanglement modifications that occur at the state level without directly displaying them. Furthermore, we observed that these representations provide access to entanglement-related information even in systems where entanglement is absent. Complementarily, the tomographic format revealed quantum synchronization in the mode mixing of a single entangled state, a phenomenon that typically lacks significance in classical contexts. The utility of this method for investigating entanglement and associated quantum characteristics in multimode systems was emphasized. Finally, we underscored the potential of electron tomography for deeper explorations of nonlocality and steering in the quantum realm. As a sophisticated tool, it can serve as an effective means for showcasing the limitations of local hidden variable models and for visualizing the violation of Bell and steering inequalities. Regarding practical applications, this method could find utility in the development of entanglement-based communication protocols, such as quantum key distribution. In this context, the approach would function similarly to how optical wavefunctions are utilized in related protocols, offering a viable solution for future entanglement-driven communication systems.

This study tackles the inverse problem of determining stick-slip dynamics from acoustic emission (AE) signals generated during the peeling of an adhesive tape. Neural point cloud models deliver end-to-end solutions for point cloud classification and downstream tasks. Recently, Encoding-based architectures have surpassed Decoding-based ones in accuracy, enabling the integration of Neural Point Cloud Smoothing (TPC) to enhance classification performance. Nevertheless, TPC lacks generalizability due to reliance on hand-crafted transformations like random rotation and shearing. Furthermore, existing methods do not fully explore TPC's potential beyond classification. In this study, we introduce a generalised formulation for TPC that eliminates dependence on specific transformations. Consequently, this approach remains effective even when distribution shifts occur between training and inference stages caused by varying transformations. Building on this generalised framework, we propose a novel method, Transformation-Unique Smoothing, which systematically optimises coordinates under different transformations to maximise classification accuracy. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our generalised framework outperforms current S.O.S. techniques across various transformations, while U-Smoothing consistently improves accuracy under different test conditions. Additionally, the combination of E-ARC, U-Smoothing, and TPC-Y shows significant gains over E-ARC alone, validating the value of coordinate optimisation and smoothing. These results confirm that our coordinate-based smoothing strategy is highly effective, offering a simple yet powerful alternative to training distributions. To facilitate adoption, we open-sourced the code at https://github.com/your-repo/tpc.

Software testing holds significant value for enhancing the reliability of real-world systems, yet effective strategies remain limited. This work introduces a geometric framework for unit testing that identifies optimal sets of test cases aimed at maximizing code coverage. We present an algorithm to determine the minimal collection of coverage criteria required to achieve specified code coverage goals. Applying Helly's theorem, we establish that achieving 99% line coverage for structural criteria demands at least 1,200 tests, while 95% branch coverage requires a minimum of 20,000 tests. Conversely, 100% coverage for any combination of structural criteria can be accomplished with far fewer executions. These findings highlight the practical benefits of incorporating 100% line and branch coverage into acceptance testing to validate the code coverage objectives of mass-tested unit systems. Additionally, this geometric method offers a pedagogical tool for computer science education to illustrate the challenges of maximizing code coverage. The algorithm has been implemented in an open-source library available at https://github.com/SHRIVASTAVA-AMAN/structural-criteria-. The codebase includes implementations across C/C++, Java, Python, and Go. Empirical results from this implementation are detailed in the accompanying paper. This research serves as an update to the arXiv:1909.09905 paper, featuring implementations for the C# language and refined implementations for C/C++ and Java. Furthermore, we provide a geometric visualization for control flow graphs (CFG) of programs in selected source languages, as demonstrated in this demo.

This paper presents a novel approach to establishing the existence of Serre weights for $\GL_2$, utilizing Kummer theory in place of classical ramified local field theory. While this method does not yield new existence results for standard Serre weights, it offers an alternative perspective that enables quicker proofs of certain outcomes and simplifies some arguments. Most significantly, the author extends this framework to define and investigate the existence of 2-adic lifts for "most" irreducible mod 2 representations, even when these representations are not semisimple. Generalizing further, the work considers a definition of Serre weights applicable to any finite reductive local overgroup $G_f$ of a fixed p-adic Lie group $T_1$, proposing corresponding existence results for such broader weights. Along the way, the author also provides simplified proofs for several related findings.

This study presents a novel framework for exact damage shaping in self-sensing composite materials via electrical impedance tomography (ZIT) and genetic algorithms (GA). While self-sensing composites, particularly carbon-fiber-reinforced polymers (CFRPs), enable non-contact damage detection through methods like electrical tomography (ET), they lack capabilities for precise damage localization and shaping. Consequently, industry adoption has been hindered by the absence of effective post-damage localization and shaping technologies. Genetic algorithms are employed to determine the optimal tapping points and central electrode polarity switches required to localize damage at specific coordinates and configure its shape (circle, square, or triangle) without restricting material usage or damage positioning. Experimental validation was conducted on a unidirectional CFRP panel, where ZIT reconstructed damage shape and extent, while GA identified optimal excitation and sensing configurations for shape and localization. The results demonstrate that ET effectively reconstructs damage shape and size, and GA successfully determines configurations for localization and shaping. Furthermore, the integrated system of self-sensing CFRPs, ET, and GA achieves exact damage shaping and localization, with reconstructed and actual shapes showing 97% area similarity and shapes remaining within a 2-pixel margin. These findings indicate that although individual components of this framework have been explored previously, their combination constitutes a new, comprehensive approach for exact damage shaping and localization using self-sensing composites and genetic algorithms. Looking ahead, future research could involve adding layers of complexity to the damage shape, expanding the range of ET materials, and performing field trials. Additionally, replacing genetic algorithms with machine learning models could enhance damage shape and location configuration. Ultimately, this work offers significant contributions to the fields of materials science and electrical engineering regarding self-sensing composites and electrical tomography. Keyphrase: Self-sensing composites, Damage localization, Electrical Impedance Tomography, Carbon fiber reinforced polymer, Genetic Algorithms.

We introduce a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces that prioritizes rotational invariance, establishing it as a foundational principle. Within this approach, we systematically classify Euclidean tensors and define a comprehensive set of invariant geometric vectors and tensors. This collection includes the position vector, the anisotropy tensor, and various mixed products involving vectors and the anisotropy tensor. These invariant objects form the basis for a detailed analysis of coordinate transformations between different Euclidean bases. Furthermore, we explicitly formulate the rules governing the transformed coordinates of the anisotropy tensor when shifting to a specialized orthonormal basis where this tensor takes its simplest possible form. As applications of this tensor calculus, we derive the geometric components of the Laplacian and the Roto-Vector Operators, and we also examine how these components behave under rotations to a preferred orthonormal basis. To support readers, Appendix A offers a detailed summary of the main results and their derivations, while Appendix B provides a tabular overview of the geometric vectors and tensors introduced throughout this work.

We demonstrate that quasi-isometric splittings of X, generated by the right-angled Artin complex $\CA(\Gamma)$ associated with a grid-minor ordered pair of commuting diagrams $\Gamma$, induce isomorphic splittings of both $\CA(\Gamma)$ and the corresponding right-angled CAT(0) cube complex $X(\Gamma)$. Leveraging this finding, we offer simplified proofs of several results by Combet, Delgado, and  Rupright regarding the isomorphism and isotopy of right-angled CAT(0) cube complexes. Furthermore, we establish that the fundamental group of a right-angled Artin graph, which is an hcp (higher connectivity of properties) property, is an LCA (locally linearized) property. Our work also introduces an invariant for the isotopy of such complexes and defines an algorithm to construct it; utilizing this invariant, we show that two specific commuting diagrams are not isotopic. The remaining sections of this paper are dedicated to developing the invariant in Section 2, proving the main theorem in Section 3, and detailing the proof of the LCA property in Section 4. Finally, we conclude by outlining potential future directions. Notably, the concept of the invariant itself may serve as a valuable tool in other contexts, potentially even outside the study of right-angled Artin complexes.

Facilitators of Congruent Congruence Expansion (CEC) and Congruence Expansion (CE) have been employed to accelerate the inversion of large, sparse, positive definite matrices. While CEC has historically been utilized for iterative inversion methods like Newton's iteration (NI) and NI², these approaches have seen limited application beyond solving linear systems, primarily due to the computational complexity of each NI step, which scales as O(n³). Furthermore, CEC has predominantly been implemented on CPUs, where its performance benefits are constrained by high memory access costs. This document introduces a generalization of NI² adapted for GPU acceleration, termed Newton's Iteration with Congruent Congruence Expansion with Batch Inversion (NICCE-BI). Additionally, a generalization of the CEC step itself, called CEC with Batch Inversion (CEC-BI), is proposed. Numerical experiments comparing NI², NICCE-1BI, and NICCE-2BI (utilizing two blocks) demonstrate that NICCE-1BI and NICCE-2BI offer significant speedups over NI² when inverting 2000+ order matrices, with greater advantages expected for larger scales. These findings indicate that both CCE and CEC can be effectively leveraged for fast, scalable matrix inversion on GPUs. The proposed methods hold potential value in real-time seismic tomographic imaging, any application requiring Hessian inversion, and other domains benefiting from CEC. A prototype implementation is accessible at https://github.com/egill/nicce. Keywords: Congruence Congruence Expansion, Congruence Expansion, Newton's Iteration, Matrix Inversion, Seismic Tomographic Inverse Point Source Imaging, Hessian Inversion, NICCE, CEC, CCE.

Contextual linear bandits find extensive application in recommendation systems and related domains. In a realistic scenario where a single algorithm manages a massive dataset too vast for a single server, we consider a hierarchical setup: a central agent collects actions and rewards from a high-dimensional ($p$) contextual linear contextual bandit problem, delegating this task to $N$ non-centralized agents operating in parallel. This configuration represents a real-world "settlement" environment, where a central server (server A) lacks direct access to client data, and non-centralized agents (server B) handle data locally without knowledge of the problem's parametric form. We propose Learning in a Settlement Environment, the first algorithm to solve this issue in a parameter-efficient manner. Specifically, each agent learns a simple linear model independent of the high dimension $p$, requiring only $O(p/N)$ samples per agent for convergence. Theoretical findings support these claims, and extensive simulations using both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm that Learning in a Settlement Environment outperforms naive baselines like $\epsilon$-greedy and Upper Confidence Bound approaches. Simulated experiments also demonstrate the algorithm's scalability across large datasets.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism driven by the vertical profile of gas rotation velocity in protoplanetary disks. Although potentially active across most of a disk, the VSI is most prominent in the outer regions. In these areas, the gas rotation speed exceeds the Keplerian frequency, a condition reliant upon a radial rotation frequency that is flatter than Keplerian. This "super-Keplerian" state, which fuels the VSI, is most likely to emerge where mass accretion and the resulting viscous evolution have significantly slowed the gas rotation. Consequently, the VSI becomes effective only after the disk has undergone substantial viscous evolution, which also implies that the instability operates when the gas mean free path is small relative to the disk's scale height, ensuring the validity of fluid dynamics. Furthermore, VSI-generated turbulence could sustain this mean free path. While the VSI has been investigated in dust-free disks, the outer regions are characterized by large dust particles with low midplane densities and long settling times. This creates a scenario where the mean free path of substantial dust grains may exceed the local scale height, causing them to slip under differential rotation and potentially altering the VSI's efficiency. Additionally, small dust particles with short mean free paths could dampen the instability's velocity shears. Using a global, self-consistent, three-dimensional simulation, we found that both large and small dust populations reduce VSI turbulence strength by as much as 40%. Although the precise impact of dust evolution on VSI efficiency remains a subject of debate, our simulation demonstrated that large dust grains do not destabilize the VSI due to their mean free path. Moreover, we observed that the gas accretion rate increases with higher opacity and smaller midplane densities in the outer disk regions, a phenomenon attributed to the large mean free paths of dust grains. Finally, we concluded that while large dust grains sliding under differential rotation in the outer regions do not destabilize the VSI, they can enhance accretion by increasing the mean free path of smaller particles.

This study examines a Laplacian comparison theorem derived from a recent work by the first two authors, and utilizes it to establish a Liouville theorem concerning harmonic functions on Ricci shrinkers with nearly constant scalar curvature. The findings are applied to demonstrate that ancient solutions to the Ricci flow satisfying specific conditions must possess constant scalar curvature. Additionally, the results are used to prove that an eternal shrinking solution of the Ricci flow on a manifold with finite volume necessarily has constant scalar curvature. It is hoped that these outcomes will contribute to a complete classification of gradient shrinking solitons in future research. Furthermore, the related concepts and principal results are explored in detail by the first author in a separate paper [10]. The analysis in that work also incorporates several new results, which, when combined with the outcomes of this paper, will facilitate the proof of the main theorem in [10]. Finally, some of the results presented in [10] will complement the work described in this article.

The rise of outsourced inference models, such as public API-based image classifiers, has intensified the threat posed by malicious backdoor attacks. Recently, Feng et al. (arXiv:2009.10887) demonstrated that neural network defenses previously considered effective against standard backdoor attacks can be circumvented by dynamic backdoors with globally activated trigger images. In this work, we further illustrate that such dynamic backdoors can be implemented with trigger images that are themselves backdoored, forming a hierarchical structure. We call this novel attack type a "global backdoor." Experimentally, we show that common data cleaning methods, including the recently introduced NTB technique by Feng et al., fail to mitigate global backdoors. Furthermore, we prove that a dominant global backdoor can even override a carefully optimized local backdoor within a clean dataset. Addressing these threats, we introduce a new defense strategy and a corresponding detection method. Specifically, we adapt the state-of-the-art "warping" defense (Ruan et al., USEUX 2020) to expose hidden trigger images during the inference stage, thereby preventing both local and global backdoor activations. Our experiments indicate that warping successfully neutralizes various local backdoor patterns under different architectures and poisoning strategies, as well as multiple global backdoor configurations. Similarly, when facing state-of-the-art detectable local backdoors, successful deployments of global backdoors—even with significantly larger poisoned datasets—can be identified. Finally, we demonstrate that warping remains effective against dynamic global backdoors, even when the trigger image exhibits natural-looking features designed to deceive downstream consumers of the cleaned data. Regarding the specific attack parameters, our findings reveal that a global backdoor dataset need not be large; in some scenarios, images from a completely clean dataset can even function as the global trigger. Conversely, the associated hideout (the local backdoor) requires a minimum size of approximately 300 images. These results underscore the challenging nature of mitigating and detecting global backdoor attacks. To combat this, we propose a practical guideline: before applying any defense against local backdoors, one must first expose and remove potential global backdoor contaminants. All datasets and code required to reproduce this study are available at https://drive.google.com/file/d/1qQhW70000000000000000000000000/view.

This work addresses the challenge of federated learning (FL) under data distribution shifts, aiming to train a global model for multi-task classification from heterogeneous data. Moving beyond standard mean-gradient-based methods, which demand high costs and are constrained by severe distribution shifts, we propose Learnful Strolling (LFS), a random walk (RW)-based learning framework. Within LFS, data access and updates occur simultaneously as a "strolling" agent visits local devices. By formulating this process as a Markov decision process (MDP), we design an optimal policy to maximize utility, defined as the sum of data volume, communication savings, and model accuracy. Exploiting the state-space and action-space characteristics of this MDP, we derive an optimal linear policy parameterized by a value function. We further derive a novel loss function considering data heterogeneity and derive its optimal weight. Extensive experiments across synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that LFS effectively utilizes data for decision-making and significantly outperforms baseline approaches in terms of utility, accuracy, and other key metrics. Code is accessible at: https://github.com/abhishek-97/LFS.

This study presents a simplicity regularization approach designed to enhance the generalization of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) within labeled and semi-supervised medical image segmentation tasks. By integrating this method with adversarial classification, we developed a model that effectively counters overfitting on the small, Lennard-Jones molecular assembly, where simple supercells are placed at high densities to minimize energy. yielding improved segmentation quality against adversarial noise and demonstrating superior generalization for unseen simple LENNARD-JONES atomic configurations. Ultimately, the framework achieves the highest performance on fully unsupervised datasets, yielding significant gains over state-of-the-art solutions on both real medical image datasets and the LENNARD-JONES molecular dataset. Furthermore, the approach maintains robustness against adversarial attacks, ultimately delivering the most effective performance on completely unsupervised data, and opens new possibilities for segmenting medical images without labeled examples. Furthermore, the method proves effective against distortions, noise, and adversarial attacks ultimately achieving state-of-the-art results on fully unsupervised datasets. Ultimately, the approach delivers peak performance on completely unsupervised data and holds potential for new applications in segmenting medical images that lack labeled components. Ultimately, this method proves beneficial for addressing challenges related to medical images with absent segmentation labels. In this letter, we introduced a consistency regularization strategy for semi-supervised medical image segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art results on a 3D brain tumor dataset and the LENNARD-JONES molecular segmentation dataset without accessing ground truth for the unlabeled portion. Ultimately, this consistency regularization framework for deep CNNs offers a valuable, standalone addition to existing adversarial approaches, potentially benefiting other medical image segmentation tasks. Specifically, this framework can assist in analyzing medical images that are missing ground truth labels, potentially creating new opportunities for datasets where annotated segments are absent. Ultimately, this consistency regularization framework for deep CNNs provides a valuable, standalone contribution to existing adversarial methods, potentially aiding other medical image segmentation tasks, especially those lacking access to ground truth segments. At the heart of quantum foundations lie nonlocal effects, most notably demonstrated through the EPR effect and violations of Bell inequalities. These phenomena arise from the counterintuitive nature of entanglement. We investigate whether a similarly striking effect, steering, can emerge from single-particle entanglement. We establish the existence of genuine single-particle nonlocality by showing that steering, which is strictly more powerful than entanglement, can occur in previously unrecognized forms of single-particle entanglement. Consequently, we prove the existence of at least three distinct nonlocal effects, ranging from the most conventional (inequality violations) to the most extreme (genuine nonlocality), and we provide the first proof that single-particle entanglement is genuinely nonlocal. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this entanglement enables truly amazing feats of telepathy via single-particle steering. To achieve this, we develop a formalism for analyzing single-particle entanglement and nonlocality, which may also benefit related fields such as quantum optics and the foundations of quantum theory. Specifically, this approach could help resolve longstanding controversies regarding the nonlocality of local single-mode laser light and the single-particle Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen entanglement. Our findings confirm that single-particle entanglement produces remarkable nonlocal phenomena, effectively "rubbing noses" with magic realism. These results underscore the incredible, counterintuitive character of single-particle entanglement and its associated nonlocality, reinforcing the validity of the EPR argument that quantum mechanics implies nonlocality and highlighting the unique significance of single-particle nonlocality. This concept could prove particularly valuable in advancing research on the relationship between nonlocality and realism.

Although the integration of 5G and emerging 6G technologies has advanced communication systems, Internet of Vehicles (IoV) applications continue to face significant data-centric challenges, including data silos, privacy concerns, and high transmission costs. Consequently, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising solution for IoV. However, the volatile and transient nature of IoV, coupled with limited on-board storage and computational resources in vehicles, introduces additional hurdles to large-scale deployment. Blockchain technology offers a mechanism to ensure data integrity and security within FL frameworks for IoV; nonetheless, its inclusion adds latency and increases storage and computational overhead. To address these issues and enable the practical implementation of FL for IoV, this paper presents a comprehensive survey proposing three novel approaches: model-centric, data-centric, and hybrid-centric Frameworks. Furthermore, we outline key challenges and suggest potential solutions for FL-IoV applications. Finally, we propose a future roadmap for standardizing these solutions to facilitate the widespread adoption of Blockchain and FL technologies in IoV environments. This work is titled: A Survey on Blockchain Empowered Federated Learning Framework for Internet of Vehicles (\textbf{SFLIB}). The accompanying repository can be accessed at: https://github.com/SFLI-ULIB/Block empowered FL for Iov. The authors are: Wasi Ahmed, Rajiv Singh, and Tanmay Panthi.

Long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks are widely employed in video analysis tasks, including video identification, due to their exceptional performance in processing temporal data. However, the substantial computational demands of LSTMs create significant barriers to both effective deployment and increased model complexity within real-time video identification scenarios. This paper introduces an algorithmic and hardware-co-designed approach for energy-efficient LSTMs specifically targeted at resource-constrained edge devices. The strategy begins with an algorithmic cohort through a novel, lossless hierarchical tensor decomposition (HTD) method, which compresses LSTM weights and biases. Subsequently, a hardware design leveraging multiplexers (MUX) and adders (ADD) was created to execute the HTD-LSTM computations. Validating this approach, a video identification system was constructed using the compressed HTD-LSTM models and the specialized hardware circuit. Comparative evaluations against standard LSTM-based models and a real-time edge device (NVIDIA Jetson Nano) demonstrate that the HTD-LSTM system achieves higher accuracy while consuming 2.15 to 10 times less energy. Furthermore, the hardware-co-design enables the execution of a 1080p video stream at a rate of 9.02 frames per second using HTD-LSTM models with an compression ratio of 21:1. Finally, the proposed algorithmic and hardware-co-design framework for energy-efficient LISTS was also applied to a speech identification task, yielding similarly favorable outcomes. This study explores the connection between the iterates of the composition of polynomials and prime characterization, presenting a novel approach to characterizing specific prime numbers. Additionally, we introduce the concept of the $p$-th order iterate of the composition of polynomials for any prime $p$, demonstrating its utility in characterizing prime factors of binomials and in establishing properties regarding the existence of the $p$-th root of the binomial $x^n + q$ (where $q$ is an integer). Furthermore, we defined the $F$-th order iterate for when $F$ is a natural number and highlighted its potential in characterizing primes. The concept of the $a$-th order iterate of the binomial $x^b + c$ was introduced for natural numbers $a$ and integers $b$ and $c$, with applications in characterizing primes and identifying Diophantine solutions. Finally, we defined the $(F,a)$-th order iterate, combining the $F$-th and $a$-th iterates, and applied it to characterize primes and determine Diophantine solutions for the equation $X^ n - Y^ m = C$, where $n,$ $m,$ and $C$ are natural numbers. The research suggests that the $(F,a)$-th order iterate of the binomial $x^ b + c$ (for $b > 1$) can be utilized to address the Hilbert-Egyptian Fraction Problem. Specifically, the (2,3)-th order iterate of $x^4 + 2$ was employed to confirm that 1989 cannot be expressed as the sum of four distinct unit fractions, and the (2,5)-th order iterate of $x^6 - 1$ was applied to demonstrate that $X^5 - Y^4 = 1989$ has no integer solutions. These findings indicate that this framework can also be used to characterize the Diophantine problem of determining whether $X^ n - Y^ m = C$ possesses solutions with $n > 2$ and $m > 2$, an issue linked to the Erdős-Sierpinski Conjecture on $X^ n - Y^ m = C$ for $n > 2$ and $m > 2$. This paper examines the Schr\"odinger equation defined on the region outside a smooth, compact, convex obstacle in $\R^d$ ($d\geq 1$), subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. We demonstrate that the singularity time $T_s$ of the solution corresponds precisely to the existence of a global energy-balls trajectory. Furthermore, assuming the obstacle is strictly convex, we establish the global existence of solutions for initial conditions whose $H^1$-norm is sufficiently small. The proof relies on a refined version of the strategy proposed by Carlen, Levine, and Sire [6] for the case of no obstruction, combined with a novel application of geometric optics. Our findings indicate that the curvature of the obstacle boundary can counteract nonlinear effects; specifically, in the context of plasma confinement, the presence of a convex wall can mitigate explosive singularities arising from non-global existence, potentially offering advantages over scenarios without such a wall. Regarding the shape of the obstacle, a more acute curvature yields stronger mitigation effects. These conclusions extend to obstacles with multiple flat faces, provided the associated Gram matrix is negative definite. However, we also show that the presence of a face with non-negative curvature can compensate for this, preventing explosive singularities. Ultimately, our results align with and utilize the strategy from the work by Germain, Metivier, and Szeftel [5] concerning wave equations on globally hyperbolic manifolds.

This work demonstrates that varieties over finitely produced Q-algebras possessing a local-atomic characteristic-zero reduction (not necessarily finite) can be varied to exhibit local-atomic semi-parametric local-uniform reductions in positive characteristic. Specifically, we establish a local-atomic version for varieties defined on a finitely produced Q-algebra that already admits such a semi-parametric local-uniform reduction. As an application, we provide a new proof of the Mostowski-Model Theorem regarding the model completeness of logically generic varieties over finitely produced Q-algebras with a local-atomic local-uniform reduction in positive characteristic, utilizing the aforementioned semi-parametric reduction. Furthermore, we outline potential directions for future research. The concepts of "local-atomic" and "local-uniform" local-characteristic reductions are introduced here for the first time, representing a novel contribution. These notions serve as a non-asymmetric replacement for "first-order" and "first-order with parameters" characteristic-p reductions, enabling the development of a "local-atomic model theory" (or "local model theory") in characteristic p (or locally). This framework offers an alternative to the existing asymptotic model theory (also known as pseudo-finite model theory) when working with varieties over finitely produced Q-algebras. Consequently, this local-atomic model theory can be integrated with Grothendieck's topos theory (and its associated Grothendieck semantics) to construct a topos-model theory of set-theoretic large varieties (and their Grothendieck semantics). Such a construction could potentially yield proofs of results in set-theoretic large model theory for varieties over finitely produced Q-algebras, which are challenging to address using standard first-order or large model theory approaches. Such varieties, equipped with a positive-characteristic semi-parametric local-uniform reduction, would require an analogy to "small" anabelian geometry over p-adic fields featuring a "small" Grothendieck topology (and corresponding Grothendieck semantics) tailored to these varieties and their reductions. In this context, a "local-atomic anabelian conjecture" over such a topology and varieties could be investigated. Notably, this conjecture might be resolvable for specific sets of primes p, given the availability of a "local-atomic anabelian theory" for these varieties and their local-atomic positive-characteristic (semi-parametric) local-uniform reductions.

Hypothesis testing is a fundamental component of cognitive science, with Bayes factors offering a primary method for evaluating hypotheses based on evidence. Although widely employed, the reliance on Bayes factors remains controversial due to the sensitivity of results toward the prior probabilities assigned to the hypotheses being compared. To address this, this study presents a workflow designed to enhance the robustness of conclusions drawn from Bayes factors during data analysis. Central to this approach is the examination of prior sensitivity across multiple Bayesian methods simultaneously. Additionally, the communicative value of such analyses is improved by visualizing the specific combinations of prior probabilities in each hypothesis that yield identical Bayes factor outcomes. This workflow was applied to assess competing models in a perceptual discrimination task, revealing considerable sensitivity in the Bayes factors for the current data. Ultimately, prioritizing the prior probabilities of hypotheses as a focal metric of evidential strength facilitated more informed decisions regarding the support provided by the data for each model. To support this, a free, user-friendly R package implementing this workflow, named 'priorworkflow', is available at https://github.com/julianjasp/priorworkflow. Furthermore, an open-access dataset allowing readers to replicate the study's analysis is located at https://osf.io/y362e.

This work does not require adherence to any specific philosophical stance on Bayesian statistics to utilize the described workflow. However, the underlying calculations are strictly Bayesian in nature, relying on the probabilistic formulation of likelihoods and treating prior probabilities as quantitative inputs. Consequently, the workflow can be adapted to analyze any dataset using any set of competing Bayesian models, whether hierarchical Bayesian models from cognitive neuroscience, non-Bayesian models assigned Bayesian priors, or other applicable frameworks. While the specific prior probabilities of hypotheses will vary depending on the research context and contextually appropriate expectations, the workflow serves as a valuable tool for strengthening the evidential support of data against competing hypotheses and for evaluating the reasonableness of prior probability assignments within a given context. Finally, although this workflow is designed for Bayesian data analysis, its conclusions should be integrated into a broader research program that considers other relevant evidence, such as the cogency of hypotheses within the specific domain and prior support for a model's structural and mathematical assumptions. Such contextual evidence is essential for ultimately assigning a quantitative measure of support to a model's prior probability.

Discourse markers, such as $\it{thus}$ and $\it{by contrast}$, signal specific semantic relationships between clauses, a function that is critical for human comprehension but difficult for machines to acquire. While recent attempts have been made to enable systems like machines and robots to learn discourse marker meanings from textual data, these approaches lack empirical support from standard natural language processing tasks. Furthermore, concurrent efforts to allow robots to infer meanings from video remain limited to specific markers, handpicked datasets, and controlled environments. To bridge these gaps, we introduce DiscSense, an system that facilitates the acquisition of semantics for discourse markers across different modalities and datasets through a comprehensive framework. Utilizing this system, we conducted a series of experiments where a robot absorbed the meanings of markers from both language and video. The results indicate that the DiscSense framework supports effective learning of discourse marker semantics from multiple data sources, yielding outcomes that surpass those of previous methods. The code for DiscSense is accessible at \url{https://github.com/linguee/DiscSense}.

This paper introduces a unified family of deformations that generalize both the Jordanian and Drinfel'd twist solutions to the 2D Euclidean renormalization group. We demonstrate that the Drinfel'd twist form for the $\mathcal{R}_- $ Lie algebra and the Jordanian expolicitor form for $r_{-}$ are related through a specific, non-trivial conjugation involving a further Lie algebra element. Additionally, we generalize the Drinfel'd twist coprope diagrammatic calculus to encompass the new unified family. Utilizing this extended calculus, we derive explicit expressions for the unified family in terms of $\mathcal{R}_- $, highlighting the significance of the relation between the $R$-matrix and the operator $\gamma$ of right multiplication by the deformation parameter. We also establish explicit formulas linking this family to $r_{+}$ and provide coproperp representations of the associated 2-cocycle. Finally, we present coproperp formulations of these families in terms of both $r_{-}$ and $r_{+}$.

This paper introduces a novel approach to the betweenness problem for extended regular expressions, which include intersection and complement operations. We introduce the concept of multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics to enhance the observational capabilities and economic feasibility of wide-field X-ray monitors. Utilizing simple 2D mock-up systems, we demonstrate that MuLE configurations can substantially broaden the effective field of view per mirror and elevate spectral resolution through a "binaural" approach. We present a study comparing two methodologies for determining dark matter halo mass function (MF) within dark matter-only simulations. The first involves counting individual halo instances, while the second utilizes a machine learning approach to identify hales via a "cosmic speed field" (CSF), which represents the ratio of particle velocity to resolution. Focusing on DF200 and MUFOC simulations, we derived the MF from the CSF using both gravity-based identification and our learning-based method, confirming they align closely above $10^{11}$ M$\sun$. However, significant deviations occur at lower masses, a trend we attribute to noise in the CSF at high velocities. To investigate this, we examined the MF relative to the peak velocity ($v_{\rm max}$), observing shifts with variations in both simulation resolution and the velocity cutoff ($v_{\rm cut}$). Consequently, we introduced a correction to the CS-based MF1($v_{\rm cut}$) to account for halo misses caused by this cutoff, ensuring consistency with the gravity-based MF. Ultimately, the corrected CS-based MF2($v_{\rm cut}$) serves as a robust, efficient tool for analyzing dark matter halo masses in simulations and potential future observations. Furthermore, we extracted the amplitude of the matter power spectrum ($\sigma_8$) and halo concentration-c parameter ($c_{p}$) from the MF2 via our neural network, demonstrating that this approach remains reliable even when simulated halo masses are truncated by velocity or density cutoffs. This work delivers a comprehensive analysis of the MF2 through a neural network based on the CSF in dark matter simulations, offering valuable insights for future research. Specifically, the open-source code implementing this2 method, named FINE2, is available at https://github.com/subhobhattacharjee/FINE2, complementing our earlier report on deriving the MF1 from density-based 21cm simulations \cite{subho_NAUCAT_2024}.

Detecting magnetic fields with SQUIDs has long served as a gold standard for high-sensitivity measurements. Given atomic interferometry's rising potential as a leading alternative to squid-magnetometers, there is significant value in demonstrating its sensitivity alongside established methods. This work presents the first evidence of sensitivity driven by the Meissner effect in a superconducting slab, which shields the underlying magnetic field from the interferometer's sensing area. By eliminating the need for direct field exposure at the sensing location, this approach could enable detection of fields as low as 1 fT, representing a tenfold improvement over current generation atom-interferometers. Further enhancements through optimized experimental designs could ultimately achieve sensitivities in the sub-femtotessla range. Ultimately, this research highlights how modifying the magnetic environment via the Meissner effect and altering physical setups can push detection limits beyond initial constraints, a principle applicable to various magnetometer types. Ultimately, this study emphasizes that by harnessing the Meissner effect and refining configurations, the detection thresholds of different magnetometer systems can be significantly extended.

We introduce a fully relativistic, first-principles theoretical framework designed to investigate the orbital and spin structure of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states. To validate this approach, we target a specific magnetic adatom (Co, Fe, or Cr) alongside non-magnetic ones (Mn and Pt) on the Nb(110) surface, scenarios where the coexistence of magnetic moments and YSR states within the same local environment creates a complex picture. By decomposing the YSR wave function, we demonstrate that spin-polarization induced by the Nb conduction electrons dominates over the inherent spin-polarization of the adatom's local magnetic moment in determining the YSR state's character. Consequently, for non-magnetic Mn adatoms and clusters, a genuine spin-polarized YSR state emerges only when both the local magnetic moment and its associated wave function are present. Our findings offer a comprehensive understanding of the orbital and spin composition of YSR states on magnetic adatoms situated on an s-d hybridizing surface. This framework provides a robust tool for experimentally distinguishing coexisting YSR states and local magnetic moments on magnetic adatoms via their distinct responses to superconducting surface gap modifications, whether induced by chemical co-adatom introduction or surface transformation. Furthermore, this method presents a reliable technique for discriminating between YSR states and Kondo resonances on magnetic adatoms through their differential responses to superconducting gap variations. The implemented technique utilizes scanning tunneling spectroscopy on a (110) Niobium surface.

This study demonstrates that the invariant surfaces discussed in Reference 1 do not exist within fractional-order Lorenz systems. Additionally, we prove the nonexistence of specific invariant manifolds and curves in fractional-order Lorenz, Chua, and Chebyshev systems. Furthermore, we establish that no straight-line invariant surfaces exist in fractional-order chemical A-B systems. These findings confirm that the dynamical analyses of fractional-order systems presented in References 2 and 3 are invalid, as they rely on the premise of certain invariant surfaces existing. Consequently, when an invariant surface does not exist, its dynamics cannot be accurately described, rendering such analyses meaningless. To address this gap, we conduct a rigorous dynamical dynamics order-by-order for the Lorenz system. Our results show that, aside from the integer-order chaotic dynamics, no other significant dynamics occur in the fractional-order Lorenz system. These conclusions provide a foundation for further investigation into the dynamics of fractional-order systems. These findings also carry important implications for the theory of chaotic dynamics in fractional-order systems and for applications involving control and synchronization of such systems. Regarding the terminology used, the phrase "is chaotic" in Reference 1 indicates a researcher's conjecture about a system's dynamics, derived from numerical simulations and stability analyses, which were conducted under the assumption that certain invariant surfaces exist. Similarly, the use of "invariant" in References 2 and 3 implies that these researchers treated the surfaces from Reference 1 as truly invariant within fractional-order systems, assuming their existence without further justification. In contrast, this work aims to analyze the actual dynamics of fractional-order systems, rather than those of the surfaces themselves. We adopt the term "invariant" for surfaces that remain unchanged (i.e., $f(\xi,\eta,\zin t)=0$ implies $f(\xi,\eta,\zint +1)=0$) under the flow of fractional-order systems, even if they do not strictly exist as invariant surfaces in such systems. These findings align with the conclusions in Reference 4, which investigated the existence of limit cycles in fractional-order systems and determined that the Poincaré-Bendixson Theorem is not applicable, concluding similarly that the invariants surfaces from Reference 1 do not exist in fractional-order contexts. While this paper focuses on the nonexistence of invariant surfaces in fractional-order dynamical systems, this issue represents a significant challenge when applying the Poincaré-Bendixson Theorem or its generalizations to analyze the dynamics of such systems.

This research demonstrates the feasibility of an inverse problem concerning the driver action in an electrodynamic transducer (EDT) for acoustic shaming. The objective is to determine the phase response required in the EDT to counteract structural vibration caused by an acoustic excitation (acoustic shaming). While both direct and inverse problems involving acoustic-structure-EDT systems have been theoretically discussed, this study provides the first experimental verification for both scenarios. The specific configuration involves an EDT placed in front of a conical bell, which is simultaneously subjected to an acoustic input and an electrical input (in the direct problems) or solely an acoustic input (in the inverse problem). The experiments confirm that the inverse problem is theoretically practical but remains highly challenging to execute successfully. Furthermore, the data generated during this work will serve as the foundation for future research into more complex direct and inverse problems, including those that account for uncertainties related to boundary conditions, excitation characteristics, and measurement noise.

We introduce the simplest non-standard scoto-seesaw model featuring an inverted spectral ordering, where the lighter neutrino mass eigenstate corresponds to the heavier state. Although achieving the precise atmospheric neutrino mass splitting $\Delta m_{atm}^{2}$ typically demands new physics at TeV scales, we demonstrate that precision is possible even with seesaw-scale mechanisms. Within this framework, we analyze the phenomenology of the invisible Higgs decay and vacuum stability, detailing how to accommodate the measured scalar spectrum while maintaining a metastable vacuum up to the Planck scale. We explicitly map out the parameter space that satisfies all constraints, including direct searches for heavy neutral states. Furthermore, we focus on the scenario where the second and third neutrino mass eigenstates are degenerate, exploring its implications for oscillation experiments, future colliders, and neutrinoless double beta decay experiments. Our results indicate that, to meet all constraints, the lightest neutrino mass must exceed $m_1 \gtrsim 2.2\times 10^{-2}$ eV, and the new physics scale cannot surpass $\Lambda \lesssim 1.4$ TeV. Finally, we present a mass hierarchy matrix that highlights the distinctive "zig-zag" pattern characteristic of seesaw mechanisms.
